```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4
)
set.seed(20261102)
```

```{r cran-gate, include = FALSE}
# The model fits below are evaluated when the article is built locally, in CI
# and for the pkgdown site (all of which set NOT_CRAN). CRAN's check farm gives
# the whole check a ten-minute budget, which these fits do not fit inside, so
# there the code is shown without being run.
EVAL_FITS <- identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = EVAL_FITS)
# Read here, not in a gated chunk: chunk options are evaluated whether or not
# the chunk runs, so a flag a chunk option reads has to exist either way.
has_lme4    <- requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)
has_glmmTMB <- requireNamespace("glmmTMB", quietly = TRUE)
has_inla    <- requireNamespace("INLA", quietly = TRUE)
has_cmdstan <- requireNamespace("cmdstanr", quietly = TRUE) &&
  !is.null(tryCatch(cmdstanr::cmdstan_version(), error = function(e) NULL))
has_brms    <- requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE) &&
  (has_cmdstan || requireNamespace("rstan", quietly = TRUE))
```

Four packages shaped how a mixed or latent Gaussian model is written and
fitted in R. [lme4](https://github.com/lme4/lme4/) (Bates et al. 2015)
introduced the `(1 + x | g)` formula syntax for random effects and fits
generalized linear mixed models by maximum likelihood, with a Laplace or
adaptive Gauss-Hermite approximation to the integral over each group.
[glmmTMB](https://github.com/glmmTMB/glmmTMB) keeps that syntax, computes the
Laplace approximation with automatic differentiation through TMB, and adds
families such as the negative binomial and Tweedie, zero-inflation through
`ziformula`, and restricted (REML) estimation for non-Gaussian responses.
[brms](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/) translates the same formulas into a Stan
program and samples the full posterior with the No-U-Turn sampler, with priors
set per parameter class. INLA (Rue, Martino and Chopin 2009) computes posterior
marginals for latent Gaussian models by nested Laplace approximations, writes
each structured effect as an `f()` term, and supplies the penalised-complexity
(PC) priors and the scaled BYM2 areal model that tulpa uses as its defaults.

tulpa takes the lme4 formula syntax and the INLA latent blocks into one
Bayesian engine. Blocks that a deterministic approximation handles well are
fitted by Laplace or nested Laplace, as in INLA, and the directions where that
approximation is biased can be corrected by exact sampling, as in Stan. The fit
records which method ran. This article checks that, with matched model,
settings and priors, tulpa gives the same estimates as each of the four
packages, and documents the places where it does not. Each comparison runs on
one simulated data set, so it shows agreement of the numbers on that data set
and says nothing about calibration over repeated data, which the
[Simulation-based calibration](sbc.html) article covers.

Installation is covered in [Get started](tulpa.html). The comparisons need
lme4, glmmTMB and brms from CRAN, and INLA, which is not on CRAN; its
DESCRIPTION names the repository `https://inlabru-org.r-universe.dev`. Every
chunk that calls another package runs only when that package is installed. The
brms fit uses cmdstanr as its Stan backend when CmdStan is set up, and rstan
otherwise.

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(tulpa)
```

## How agreement is measured

A comparison is only meaningful when both packages fit the same model to the
same data and report the same quantity. Each section below states three things
before its fits: the model, the estimand (maximum likelihood, restricted
likelihood or a posterior summary) and, for the Bayesian fits, the priors on
every parameter. Where one of these cannot be matched, the section says so and
the table shows the gap that follows.

Agreement is reported per parameter as the difference between the tulpa
estimate and the other package's, in the parameter's units and in units of
the other package's standard error or posterior SD. A difference of 0.01 SD
is numerical noise; a difference of 0.5 SD changes what a reader would
conclude. The helper below builds that table from two named vectors of
estimates and two of standard errors.

```{r agree-helper}
agree <- function(est_t, se_t, est_o, se_o) {
  data.frame(tulpa = est_t, tulpa_se = se_t, other = est_o, other_se = se_o,
             diff = est_t - est_o, diff_in_se = (est_t - est_o) / se_o)
}
```

To check agreement on your own data, fit the model in both packages with the
settings of the matching section, pass the estimates and standard errors to
`agree()`, and read the last column.

## Random-intercept GLMM: tulpa, lme4 and glmmTMB

A binary response measured in 40 groups of 8 is the setting where the Laplace
approximation to a group's integral is least accurate, so it is a demanding
first test. The intercept is -0.4, the slope 0.9, and the group intercepts are
drawn with SD 0.8.

```{r sim-glmm}
G <- 40L; npg <- 8L
g <- rep(seq_len(G), each = npg)
x <- rnorm(G * npg)
u <- rnorm(G, sd = 0.8)
y <- rbinom(G * npg, 1, plogis(-0.4 + 0.9 * x + u[g]))
d <- data.frame(y = y, x = x, g = factor(g))
```

lme4 and glmmTMB maximise the Laplace-approximated likelihood over the fixed
effects and the random-intercept SD. The tulpa backend that does the same is
`mode = "agq"`: with `n_quad = 1` its marginal is the same joint Laplace
approximation, and `tol` tightens the optimiser (the default tolerance is
discussed under [Differences](#optimiser-tolerance-of-the-agq-backend)).

```{r glmm-ml}
tm <- list()
tm$tulpa_agq <- system.time(
  f_t <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial", mode = "agq",
               control = list(n_quad = 1L, tol = 1e-10))
)[["elapsed"]]
summary(f_t)$coefficients[, 1:2]
f_t$sigma_re
```

```{r glmm-lme4, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_lme4 && has_glmmTMB}
tm$glmer <- system.time(
  f_l <- lme4::glmer(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = binomial)
)[["elapsed"]]
tm$glmmTMB <- system.time(
  f_g <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = binomial)
)[["elapsed"]]
c(logLik_tulpa = f_t$log_marginal, logLik_glmer = as.numeric(logLik(f_l)),
  logLik_glmmTMB = as.numeric(logLik(f_g)))
```

tulpa and glmmTMB reach the same log-likelihood to four decimals, and glmer's
default optimiser stops 0.0007 below it. The table therefore compares the
estimates against glmmTMB. The random-intercept SD has no standard error in
either package's default output, so its last two columns are empty.

```{r glmm-agree, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_lme4 && has_glmmTMB}
se_g <- sqrt(diag(vcov(f_g)$cond))
tab_ml <- agree(
  c(coef(f_t), sigma = f_t$sigma_re),
  c(summary(f_t)$coefficients[, "std.error"], NA),
  c(glmmTMB::fixef(f_g)$cond, sigma = sqrt(glmmTMB::VarCorr(f_g)$cond$g[1])),
  c(se_g, NA))
round(tab_ml, 5)
```

The same match holds for adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature. lme4 calls the
number of nodes `nAGQ`; tulpa calls it `n_quad`. With seven nodes the
integral over each group of eight binary responses is no longer a Laplace
approximation, and the SD estimate moves from 0.816 to 0.842 in both packages.

```{r glmm-agq7, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_lme4}
f_t7 <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial", mode = "agq",
              control = list(n_quad = 7L, tol = 1e-10))
f_l7 <- lme4::glmer(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = binomial, nAGQ = 7)
rbind(tulpa = c(coef(f_t7), sigma = f_t7$sigma_re),
      glmer = c(lme4::fixef(f_l7), sigma = attr(lme4::VarCorr(f_l7)$g, "stddev")))
```

## Random slopes: tulpa and glmmTMB

A random slope adds a covariance matrix: the intercept SD, the slope SD and
their correlation. lme4 fits it for this Poisson response as well, but
glmmTMB also offers the restricted likelihood, which is the estimand of
tulpa's empirical-Bayes backend. Simulate 60 groups of 12 counts with SDs 0.7
and 0.5 and correlation 0.4.

```{r sim-slopes}
G2 <- 60L; npg2 <- 12L
g2 <- rep(seq_len(G2), each = npg2)
x2 <- rnorm(G2 * npg2)
Sig <- matrix(c(0.49, 0.14, 0.14, 0.25), 2)
b2 <- t(t(chol(Sig)) %*% matrix(rnorm(2 * G2), 2))
y2 <- rpois(G2 * npg2, exp(0.2 + 0.5 * x2 + b2[g2, 1] + b2[g2, 2] * x2))
d2 <- data.frame(y = y2, x = x2, g = factor(g2))
```

`mode = "eb"` maximises the Laplace marginal over the covariance with the
fixed effects integrated out, which is the restricted (REML-type) estimate.
`hyperprior = "flat"` removes the default PC and LKJ prior on the covariance,
so nothing but the likelihood enters the maximisation; the fixed effects keep
the default `normal(0, 2.5)` prior, which is weak against 720 observations.
The glmmTMB call is the same formula with `REML = TRUE`.

```{r slopes-fit, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_glmmTMB}
tm$tulpa_eb <- system.time(
  s_t <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = d2, family = "poisson",
               mode = "eb", hyperprior = "flat")
)[["elapsed"]]
tm$glmmTMB_reml <- system.time(
  s_g <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = d2, family = poisson,
                          REML = TRUE)
)[["elapsed"]]
vc <- glmmTMB::VarCorr(s_g)$cond$g
tab_rs <- agree(
  c(coef(s_t), sd_int = s_t$map$sigma[1], sd_x = s_t$map$sigma[2],
    cor = s_t$map$rho),
  c(summary(s_t)$coefficients[, "std.error"], NA, NA, NA),
  c(glmmTMB::fixef(s_g)$cond, attr(vc, "stddev"),
    cor = attr(vc, "correlation")[1, 2]),
  c(sqrt(diag(vcov(s_g)$cond)), NA, NA, NA))
round(tab_rs, 5)
```

The SDs and the correlation agree to 1e-4, and the fixed effects differ by
under a hundredth of a standard error.

The Bayesian counterpart integrates over the covariance instead of fixing it
at the maximum. With `mode = "laplace"` a slope term routes to that
integration (the [Random slopes](random-slopes.html) article covers it). The
posterior medians of the two SDs equal the restricted estimates to two
decimals, and the median of the correlation is 0.52 against the restricted
0.57, inside an interval from 0.25 to 0.72.

```{r slopes-nested}
s_n <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 + x | g), data = d2, family = "poisson",
             mode = "laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
summary(s_n)$hyperparameters[1:3, c("parameter", "median", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")]
```

## Areal BYM2 model: tulpa and INLA

The BYM2 model splits a region's effect into a scaled ICAR part and an
independent part, with a total SD `sigma` and a mixing weight for the
structured share. INLA calls the weight `phi` and parameterises the scale as
a precision; tulpa calls the weight `rho` and reports `sigma` directly. Both
scale the ICAR part so that its marginal variances have geometric mean one
(Riebler et al. 2016), which `spatial_bym2()` does and INLA's
`scale.model = TRUE` does.

Simulate Poisson counts on a 10 by 10 lattice of regions with rook
adjacency, expected counts between 10 and 60, a slope of 0.4 and a field with
total SD 0.6, 70% of its variance spatially structured.

```{r sim-bym2}
nr <- 10L; K <- nr * nr
W <- matrix(0, K, K)
id <- function(i, j) (i - 1L) * nr + j
for (i in 1:nr) for (j in 1:nr) {
  if (i < nr) W[id(i, j), id(i + 1L, j)] <- W[id(i + 1L, j), id(i, j)] <- 1
  if (j < nr) W[id(i, j), id(i, j + 1L)] <- W[id(i, j + 1L), id(i, j)] <- 1
}
cx <- rep(1:nr, each = nr); cy <- rep(1:nr, nr)
s  <- as.numeric(scale(sin(cx / 3) + cos(cy / 3)))
bf <- 0.6 * (sqrt(0.7) * s + sqrt(0.3) * rnorm(K))
x3 <- rnorm(K); E <- round(runif(K, 10, 60))
y3 <- rpois(K, E * exp(-0.3 + 0.4 * x3 + bf))
d3 <- data.frame(y = y3, x = x3, E = E, region = factor(1:K), id = 1:K)
```

### Matching the priors

The priors have to be set on the INLA side to match tulpa's defaults, since
the two packages' defaults differ.

| Parameter | tulpa default | INLA default | INLA setting used here |
|---|---|---|---|
| total SD `sigma` | PC prior, P(sigma > 3) = 0.01 | `pc.prec`, P(sigma > 1) = 0.01 | `pc.prec` with `param = c(3, 0.01)` |
| mixing weight | uniform on (0, 1) | `pc`, P(phi < 0.5) = 2/3 | `logitbeta` with `param = c(1, 1)` (uniform) |
| intercept | the nested-Laplace door's own weak prior | flat | flat |
| slope | the same | normal, precision 0.001 | normal, precision 0.001 |

INLA's `pc.prec` with `param = c(U, alpha)` states P(1 / sqrt(precision) > U)
= alpha, which is the same statement as tulpa's PC prior on `sigma`. The
fixed-effect priors cannot be matched exactly, because tulpa's
nested-Laplace door refuses a supplied `beta_prior`; the conditional check
below measures how much that matters here.

```{r bym2-tulpa}
tm$tulpa_bym2 <- system.time(
  a_t <- tulpa(y ~ x + offset(log(E)) + spatial(region), data = d3,
               family = "poisson",
               spatial = spatial_bym2(W, level = "group", group_var = "region"),
               mode = "nested_laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
)[["elapsed"]]
summary(a_t)$hyperparameters[, c("parameter", "mean", "sd")]
```

```{r bym2-inla, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_inla}
hyp <- list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(3, 0.01)),
            phi  = list(prior = "logitbeta", param = c(1, 1)))
tm$inla_bym2 <- system.time(
  a_i <- INLA::inla(
    y ~ x + f(id, model = "bym2", graph = W, scale.model = TRUE,
              constr = TRUE, hyper = hyp),
    family = "poisson", E = E, data = d3, num.threads = "2:1",
    control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0, prec = 0.001))
)[["elapsed"]]
sd_marg <- INLA::inla.tmarginal(function(t) 1 / sqrt(t),
                                a_i$marginals.hyperpar[[1]])
sd_inla <- unlist(INLA::inla.zmarginal(sd_marg, silent = TRUE)[1:2])
```

```{r bym2-agree, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_inla}
hp <- summary(a_t)$hyperparameters
tab_bym2 <- agree(
  c(coef(a_t), sigma = hp$mean[1], mixing = hp$mean[2]),
  c(summary(a_t)$coefficients[, "std.error"], hp$sd),
  c(a_i$summary.fixed$mean, sd_inla[["mean"]], a_i$summary.hyperpar$mean[2]),
  c(a_i$summary.fixed$sd, sd_inla[["sd"]], a_i$summary.hyperpar$sd[2]))
round(tab_bym2, 4)
```

The slope and the total SD agree to within 0.2 posterior SD, and the mixing
weight's mean differs by 0.03, although tulpa's posterior SD for it is 0.17
against INLA's 0.13. The intercept differs by half a posterior SD, and the
next section traces that gap to the method rather than the model.

### The same model at fixed hyperparameters

Fixing `sigma` and the mixing weight removes the outer integration, so the
two packages then solve the same inner problem: the posterior of the fixed
effects and the field given the hyperparameters. In tulpa that is one cell of
the nested-Laplace grid. `prior_from_spec()` turns the `spatial_bym2()` spec
into the prior list that `tulpa_nested_laplace()` reads, and the grid is set
to the single cell `sigma = 1 / sqrt(5)`, mixing weight 0.8.

```{r bym2-cond-tulpa}
pr <- prior_from_spec(spatial_bym2(W, level = "group", group_var = "region"),
                      d3)
pr$sigma_grid <- 1 / sqrt(5); pr$rho_grid <- 0.8
c_t <- tulpa_nested_laplace(d3$y, rep(1L, K), cbind(1, d3$x), prior = pr,
                            family = "poisson", offset = log(d3$E),
                            control = list(n_threads = 2, axis_refine = "none"))
eta_t <- as.numeric(c_t$fitted_eta[1, ]) - log(d3$E)
c_t$modes[1, 1:2]
```

On the INLA side the precision is fixed at 5 and `phi` at 0.8. INLA reports
the posterior mean of the linear predictor; by default that mean includes a
variational-Bayes correction, which is switched off here and kept on below.

```{r bym2-cond-inla, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_inla}
hyp_fix <- list(prec = list(initial = log(5), fixed = TRUE),
                phi  = list(initial = qlogis(0.8), fixed = TRUE))
cond_inla <- function(vb) INLA::inla(
  y ~ x + f(id, model = "bym2", graph = W, scale.model = TRUE,
            constr = TRUE, hyper = hyp_fix),
  family = "poisson", E = E, data = d3, num.threads = "2:1",
  control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0, prec = 0.001),
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  control.inla = list(control.vb = list(enable = vb)))
c_i0 <- cond_inla(FALSE); c_i1 <- cond_inla(TRUE)
rbind(vb_off = c(c_i0$summary.fixed$mean,
                 max_abs_eta_diff = max(abs(eta_t - c_i0$summary.linear.predictor$mean))),
      vb_on  = c(c_i1$summary.fixed$mean,
                 max_abs_eta_diff = max(abs(eta_t - c_i1$summary.linear.predictor$mean))))
```

With the correction off, INLA's fixed effects equal tulpa's to within 1e-5
and the linear predictors of the 100 regions agree to within 2e-4, so
the two packages build the same model, the same scaling and the same
constraint, and the fixed-effect priors make no visible difference. With the
correction on, the intercept moves by 0.016, close to the 0.018 gap of the
full fits above. tulpa's inner solve reports the Laplace mode; INLA's default reports a
mean corrected towards the skew of the Poisson posterior. The
[Differences](#inlas-default-mean-correction) section shows the full fit
with the correction switched off.

## A brms fit of the GLMM

brms samples the posterior of the random-intercept model from the first
section. The matched tulpa fit integrates the random-intercept SD over a grid
with adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature inside each group
(`control$re_cov = "aghq"`), under the same priors:

- the fixed effects, intercept included, `normal(0, 2.5)` in both;
- the SD, tulpa's PC prior P(sigma > 3) = 0.01, which for a random-effect SD
  is an exponential with rate `-log(0.01) / 3`, written out for brms.

brms writes the intercept as an ordinary coefficient (`0 + Intercept`) so that
the `normal(0, 2.5)` prior applies to it on the same scale as in tulpa. The
sampler runs two chains of 1000 iterations, half of them warmup.

```{r brms-fit, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_brms, cache = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, results = "hide"}
rate <- -log(0.01) / 3
pri <- c(brms::set_prior("normal(0, 2.5)", class = "b"),
         brms::set_prior(sprintf("exponential(%.6f)", rate), class = "sd"))
tm_brms <- system.time(
  f_b <- brms::brm(y ~ 0 + Intercept + x + (1 | g), data = d,
                   family = brms::bernoulli(), prior = pri, chains = 2,
                   iter = 1000, warmup = 500, cores = 2, seed = 1, refresh = 0,
                   backend = if (has_cmdstan) "cmdstanr" else "rstan")
)[["elapsed"]]
```

```{r brms-tulpa}
tm$tulpa_aghq <- system.time(
  f_q <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial",
               mode = "structured",
               control = list(re_cov = "aghq", n_threads = 2))
)[["elapsed"]]
```

```{r brms-agree, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_brms}
fb <- brms::fixef(f_b)
sb <- brms::VarCorr(f_b)$g$sd
hq <- summary(f_q)$hyperparameters
tab_brms <- agree(
  c(coef(f_q), sigma = hq$mean[1]),
  c(summary(f_q)$coefficients[, "std.error"], hq$sd[1]),
  c(fb[, "Estimate"], sb[, "Estimate"]),
  c(fb[, "Est.Error"], sb[, "Est.Error"]))
round(tab_brms, 4)
```

The posterior means of the fixed effects agree to within 0.06 posterior SD and
the mean of the SD to within 0.14. The brms posterior SDs of the slope and of
the random-intercept SD are 0.016 and 0.022 larger than tulpa's. The effective sample sizes
of the brms draws set the Monte Carlo error of its means:

```{r brms-ess, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_brms}
fx <- summary(f_b)$fixed
cbind(fx[, c("Est.Error", "Bulk_ESS")],
      mcse_in_sd = 1 / sqrt(fx[, "Bulk_ESS"]))
```

A brms mean carries a Monte Carlo error of about 0.03 posterior SD here, so
the differences in the fixed-effect means are within two Monte Carlo
standard errors.

## Measured agreement

The table collects the largest difference, in units of the other package's
standard error or posterior SD, over the parameters of each comparison that
carry one.

```{r agree-all, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_lme4 && has_glmmTMB && has_inla && has_brms}
worst <- function(tab) max(abs(tab$diff_in_se), na.rm = TRUE)
data.frame(
  comparison = c("binomial GLMM, ML (glmmTMB)", "Poisson random slope, REML",
                 "Poisson BYM2 (INLA, defaults matched)", "binomial GLMM (brms)"),
  max_abs_diff_in_se = round(c(worst(tab_ml), worst(tab_rs),
                               worst(tab_bym2), worst(tab_brms)), 3))
```

## Syntax map

The tables give the tulpa equivalent of each formula term, family, structured
effect, prior and accessor of the four packages. Every tulpa function named
here is exported by tulpa `r packageVersion("tulpa")`.

### Formula terms and data

| lme4 / glmmTMB / brms | INLA | tulpa |
|---|---|---|
| <code>(1 &#124; g)</code> | `f(g, model = "iid")` | <code>(1 &#124; g)</code> |
| <code>(1 + x &#124; g)</code> | `f(..., model = "iidkd")` | <code>(1 + x &#124; g)</code> |
| <code>(1 + x &#124;&#124; g)</code> | `f(g, model = "iid")` plus `f(g2, x, model = "iid")` | <code>(1 + x &#124;&#124; g)</code> |
| <code>(1 &#124; a/b)</code>, <code>(1 &#124; a) + (1 &#124; b)</code> | one `f()` per term | the same |
| `offset(log(E))` | `E = E` (Poisson) or `offset()` | `offset(log(E))` |
| `cbind(s, n - s) ~ ...` (lme4), <code>s &#124; trials(n)</code> (brms) | `Ntrials = n` | `s ~ ...` with `n_trials = n` |
| `weights = w` | `weights = w` | `weights = w` |
| `ziformula = ~ 1` (glmmTMB) | `zeroinflatedpoisson1` family | `ziformula = ~ 1` |
| `dispformula = ~ x` (glmmTMB) | | no equivalent |
| `nAGQ = 7` (lme4) | | `mode = "agq"`, `control = list(n_quad = 7)` |
| `REML = TRUE` (glmmTMB) | | `mode = "eb"`, `hyperprior = "flat"` |

### Families

| glmmTMB / lme4 | brms | INLA | tulpa `family =` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `binomial` | `bernoulli()`, `binomial()` | `"binomial"` | `"binomial"` |
| `poisson` | `poisson()` | `"poisson"` | `"poisson"` |
| `nbinom2` | `negbinomial()` | `"nbinomial"` | `"neg_binomial_2"` |
| `nbinom1` | | | `"neg_binomial_1"` |
| `truncated_poisson`, `truncated_nbinom2` | | | `"truncated_poisson"`, `"truncated_neg_binomial_2"` |
| `gaussian` | `gaussian()` | `"gaussian"` | `"gaussian"` |
| `lognormal` | `lognormal()` | `"lognormal"` | `"lognormal"` |
| `Gamma` | `Gamma()` | `"gamma"` | `"gamma"` |
| `inverse.gaussian` | `inverse.gaussian()` | | `"inverse_gaussian"` |
| `beta_family` | `Beta()` | `"beta"` | `"beta"` |
| `betabinomial` | `beta_binomial()` | `"betabinomial"` | `"beta_binomial"` |
| `tweedie` | | `"tweedie"` | `"tweedie"` (power in `phi2`) |
| `t_family` | `student()` | | `"t"` |

`family_names()` lists the tulpa families. tulpa holds a family's dispersion
fixed at `phi` unless `estimate_phi = TRUE` under `mode = "eb"`; the other
packages estimate it by default.

### INLA `f()` terms

| INLA | tulpa |
|---|---|
| `f(id, model = "besag", graph = W)` | `spatial(region)` with `spatial = spatial_car(W, level = "group", group_var = "region")` |
| `f(id, model = "bym2", graph = W)` | `spatial(region)` with `spatial = spatial_bym2(W, level = "group", group_var = "region")` |
| `f(id, model = "besagproper", graph = W)` | `spatial = spatial_car(W, ..., proper = TRUE)` |
| `f(t, model = "rw1")`, `"rw2"`, `"ar1"` | `temporal = temporal_rw1("t")`, `temporal_rw2("t")`, `temporal_ar1("t")` |
| `f(t, model = "rw1", replicate = g)` | `temporal = temporal_rw1("t", group_var = "g")` |
| `f(s, model = spde)` with `inla.spde2.pcmatern()` | `spatial = spatial_spde(~ lon + lat, data, max_edge = ...)` |
| `f(id, model = "generic0", Cmatrix = Q)` | `latent(tgmrf(...))` |

### Priors

| Other package | tulpa |
|---|---|
| brms `set_prior("normal(0, 2.5)", class = "b")` | `beta_prior = list(mean = 0, sd = 2.5)` (the default) |
| brms `exponential(rate)` on `sd`; INLA `pc.prec` with `param = c(U, alpha)` | `re_prior = list(prior_sigma = c(U, alpha))`, rate `-log(alpha) / U` |
| brms `lkj(eta)` on `cor` | `re_prior = list(eta = eta)` |
| INLA `pc.range` / `pc.prec` in `inla.spde2.pcmatern()` | `spatial_spde(..., prior_range = , prior_sigma = )` |
| INLA `control.fixed` | the nested-Laplace door's own prior; `beta_prior` is refused there |
| a flat prior on the variance components | `hyperprior = "flat"` |

### Accessors

| Other package | tulpa |
|---|---|
| `fixef()`, `ranef()`, `VarCorr()` | `fixef()`, `ranef()`, `VarCorr()` |
| `summary()`, `confint()`, `vcov()`, `logLik()` | the same |
| `predict(newdata = , re.form = NA)` | `predict(newdata = , type = , include_field = )` |
| `simulate()` | `simulate()` |
| brms `posterior_predict()`, `pp_check()`, `bayes_R2()`, `as_draws_df()` | the same names |
| brms `loo()`, `waic()` | `loo::loo()`, `loo::waic()` methods |
| INLA `fit$summary.fixed` | `summary(fit)$coefficients` |
| INLA `fit$summary.hyperpar` | `summary(fit)$hyperparameters` |
| INLA `fit$summary.random` | `ranef()` for a random effect, `field_effects()` for a spatial field |
| INLA `fit$mlik` | `logLik()`, the log marginal likelihood on a Laplace fit |

## Differences

The differences below are design choices of tulpa, each with the code in
both packages. They follow from two decisions: every scale tulpa does not
integrate or estimate is an argument the call states, and a fit reports the
inference method that produced it.

### A random-intercept SD is conditioned on under `mode = "laplace"`

lme4 and glmmTMB estimate the random-intercept SD in every fit. In tulpa,
`mode = "laplace"` on a random-intercept model conditions on `sigma_re`, the
value the call supplies, and warns when none is supplied. The default
`mode = "auto"` and `mode = "structured"` integrate the SD instead, and
`mode = "agq"` and `mode = "eb"` estimate it.

```{r diff-sigma-re}
f_c <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial",
             mode = "laplace", sigma_re = 0.8)
coef(f_c)
VarCorr(f_c)
```

The `source` column reads `conditioned`, so the fit carries the SD it was
given. The estimated SD of the same model is in the ML table of the first
section.

### Empirical-Bayes variances are restricted estimates

`mode = "eb"` integrates the fixed effects out of the marginal likelihood
before maximising over the variances, so with `hyperprior = "flat"` it gives
the restricted estimate of glmmTMB's `REML = TRUE`, here to within 0.002. It
does not reproduce the maximum-likelihood fit of lme4 and of glmmTMB's
default, whose SD is smaller.

```{r diff-reml, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_glmmTMB}
f_e <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial", mode = "eb",
             hyperprior = "flat")
f_r <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = binomial,
                        REML = TRUE)
c(tulpa_eb = f_e$map$sigma, glmmTMB_reml = sqrt(glmmTMB::VarCorr(f_r)$cond$g[1]),
  ml = f_t$sigma_re)
```

### A dispersion is estimated only on request

glmmTMB estimates the negative-binomial size along with everything else. tulpa
holds it at `phi` by default; `estimate_phi = TRUE` under `mode = "eb"`
estimates it, again as a restricted estimate.

```{r diff-phi, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_glmmTMB}
y_nb <- rnbinom(G * npg, mu = exp(1 + 0.5 * x + u[g]), size = 2)
d_nb <- data.frame(y = y_nb, x = x, g = factor(g))
f_nb <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d_nb, family = "neg_binomial_2",
              mode = "eb", hyperprior = "flat", estimate_phi = TRUE, phi = 1)
g_nb <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d_nb,
                         family = glmmTMB::nbinom2, REML = TRUE)
c(tulpa_size = f_nb$phi, glmmTMB_size = glmmTMB::sigma(g_nb))
```

### INLA's default mean correction

INLA applies a variational-Bayes correction to the posterior mean of the
latent field by default, which the conditional check above isolated. tulpa's
nested Laplace reports the mixture of the per-cell Laplace modes. Switching
INLA's correction off brings the full fit to tulpa's numbers.

```{r diff-vb, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_inla}
a_i0 <- INLA::inla(
  y ~ x + f(id, model = "bym2", graph = W, scale.model = TRUE,
            constr = TRUE, hyper = hyp),
  family = "poisson", E = E, data = d3, num.threads = "2:1",
  control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0, prec = 0.001),
  control.inla = list(control.vb = list(enable = FALSE)))
rbind(tulpa = coef(a_t), inla_vb_on = a_i$summary.fixed$mean,
      inla_vb_off = a_i0$summary.fixed$mean)
```

The two choices answer different questions about a skewed posterior: INLA's
corrected mean moves the estimate towards the posterior mean, tulpa keeps the
Laplace centre and leaves the skew to its diagnostics and to an exact sampler.

### Incomplete rows are refused

lme4, glmmTMB and brms drop a row with a missing value under their default
`na.action`; INLA treats a missing response as a value to predict. tulpa
refuses the data, so the rows a fit uses are always the rows supplied.

```{r diff-na, error = TRUE}
d_na <- d; d_na$x[3] <- NA
tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d_na, family = "binomial", mode = "agq")
```

```{r diff-na-lme4, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_lme4}
nobs(lme4::glmer(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d_na, family = binomial))
```

### Optimiser tolerance of the AGQ backend

At its default tolerance, `mode = "agq"` stops slightly short of the maximum
on this data set: the log-likelihood is 0.0005 below glmmTMB's and the SD
differs by 0.006. The fits above set `tol = 1e-10`.

```{r diff-tol, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_glmmTMB}
f_d <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "binomial", mode = "agq",
             control = list(n_quad = 1L))
rbind(default_tol = c(logLik = f_d$log_marginal, sigma = f_d$sigma_re),
      tol_1e_10   = c(f_t$log_marginal, f_t$sigma_re),
      glmmTMB     = c(as.numeric(logLik(f_g)),
                      sqrt(glmmTMB::VarCorr(f_g)$cond$g[1])))
```

## Timings

The timings are elapsed seconds of one run of each fit above, measured on a
shared Windows 11 workstation (beast) with R 4.6.1, two threads where a
fitter takes them, with tulpa `r packageVersion("tulpa")`. The data sizes are
320 binary responses in 40 groups (GLMM), 720 counts in 60 groups (random
slope) and 100 regions (BYM2). One run of a fit under a second carries noise
of the order of its own value, so the table shows the order of magnitude and
not a ranking; it says nothing about how the packages scale to larger data.

```{r timings, eval = EVAL_FITS && has_lme4 && has_glmmTMB && has_inla && has_brms}
tm$brms <- tm_brms
data.frame(fit = names(tm), seconds = round(unlist(tm), 2), row.names = NULL)
```

The three maximum-likelihood fits of the random-intercept model take the same
time to the precision of one run. INLA fits the BYM2 model faster than tulpa's
nested Laplace. The brms time includes compiling the Stan model, which a
cached model skips on the next run, and the tulpa AGQ integration of the same
model spends its time on nine-node quadrature inside each group at every grid
cell.

## When the other package is the better choice

- lme4 for linear mixed models fitted by REML with `lmer()`, and for profile
  likelihood intervals on the variance components.
- glmmTMB when the dispersion itself depends on covariates (`dispformula`),
  or the zero-inflation part carries random effects.
- brms for distributional and non-linear models, any likelihood Stan can
  write, and exact sampling of the whole posterior with Stan's diagnostics.
- INLA for its wide range of likelihoods and `f()` models, per-region BYM2
  summaries read directly from `summary.random`, and the inlabru interface
  for spatial point processes.

All four have years of use and published validation behind them. tulpa's
agreement rests on its own test suite and on comparisons such as the ones in
this article.
